panels.rationale: Single-panel multidetector CT angiography sagittal reconstruction from an open-access article on aortic coarctation. The image visibly shows focal aortic isthmus narrowing (arrowhead) and hypertrophic intercostal and internal mammary collateral arteries (arrows), matching the caption and the coarctation-specific vocabulary entries. It is a real patient diagnostic image of untreated coarctation of the aorta with no third-party issue, so it qualifies for the library.

panels.rationale: Single posteroanterior chest radiograph from an article on severe aortic coarctation, showing the classic figure-of-3 sign and bilateral inferior rib notching directly attributed to coarctation by the caption and in-text description.
panels.attribution_text: Gutiérrez Rangel et al. Hypertension Secondary to Severe Aortic Coarctation in an Adult Patient.. Cureus 2025. doi:10.7759/cureus.86128. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Posteroanterior chest radiograph showing the “figure 3 sign,” characterized by an indentation along the contour of the thoracic aorta due to a focal coarctation with pre and poststenotic dilatation (white arrow). Rib notching is also noted bilaterally (yellow arrows), representing collateral circulation through the intercostal arteries. This finding, known as “Roesler’s sign,” is caused by erosion of the inferior borders of the ribs secondary to increased flow through enlarged collateral vessels.

findings.evidence: rib notching in the right upper zone (Black Arrows)

panels.rationale: Single-panel AP erect chest radiograph from a case report on post-stenotic aortic coarctation aneurysms. The image visibly shows black arrows marking rib notching in the right upper zone, a classic radiographic sign of aortic coarctation from enlarged intercostal collaterals, together with a large peripherally calcified descending thoracic aortic aneurysm (post-stenotic dilatation) as stated in the caption and in-text. Both manifestations are directly captioned and the article title confirms the disease attribution to coarctation of the aorta. No other disease, diagram, control or third-party issue is present. B: Sagittal/oblique MIP CT angiography reconstruction (panel B) from the same human patient, showing the focal narrowing at the aortic isthmus (red arrow) distal to the left subclavian artery with surrounding collateral vessels, consistent with the captioned diagnosis of aortic coarctation. Both panels are real patient CT images directly showing the configured disease.

in_text_mentions: By day 2, the infant required invasive ventilation due to increased oxygen needs. Femoral pulses remained normal, SpO₂ was stable, and BP measurements showed no differential. However, PI readings were 1.20 pre-ductal and 0.23 post-ductal (Table 2). Echocardiography at 36 hours revealed a small "gothic" aortic arch with slight hypoplasia of the transverse and descending aorta and developing CoA flow (Figure 5). Prostaglandin E1 infusion was initiated, and the diagnosis of CoA was confirmed. Despite undergoing corrective surgery on day 12, the newborn died from complications one month later.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Transthoracic echo subcostal sagittal pulsed Doppler of the abdominal aorta shows a low-amplitude systolic waveform with persistent diastolic gradient (diastolic run-off), a classic downstream Doppler manifestation of significant aortic coarctation in this adolescent case. B: Parasternal short-axis echo shows concentric left ventricular hypertrophy. In this article the LVH is the pressure-overload consequence of the coarctation-associated secondary hypertension in an adolescent, so it is attributable to the coarctation, but it is a non-specific secondary finding and is therefore captured as a proposed finding rather than a vocabulary term. C: Suprasternal continuous-wave Doppler demonstrates a high-velocity turbulent jet (4.62 m/s) with an 86-85 mmHg peak gradient and continuous antegrade diastolic flow (diastolic run-off), the textbook echo signature of aortic isthmus coarctation.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (a, b, c). a: Gross specimen photo of the resected saccular pseudoaneurysm from an adult patient with untreated coarctation of the aorta; the disease-focused article title and caption directly link the aneurysm to the coarctation site, establishing attribution. The pseudoaneurysm represents aneurysmal dilatation associated with the coarctation (vocabulary synonym 'post-stenotic aneurysm'). The article describes this as a rare case, so the presentation is atypical. [raw subtype: adult] b: Elastica van Gieson histology of the resected pseudoaneurysm wall from the coarctation site in an adult with untreated coarctation; shows a clearly thinner wall with absent intima and media and elastic-fiber layers, consistent with an adventitia-only pseudoaneurysm. No vocabulary key matches (the media is absent rather than hypertrophied and the intima is absent rather than fibroelastotic), so the observations are placed in proposed_findings. Rare/atypical...

in_text_mentions: he aneurysm mass atrophied easily after clamping (Fig. 2). The saccular aneurysm lacked a defined intima and was formed of a thin single-layered membrane, which was indicative of the adventitia (Fig. 3a). The anastomosis was performed with a 20-mm 1-branch tubular graft (J Graft SHIELD NEO®, Japan Lifeline Co., Ltd. Tokyo, Japan). A drain was placed in the left thoracic cavity. The operative and cardiopulmonary bypass time were 194 and 58 min, respectively. In addition, the aortic block time, minimum body temperature and bleeding volume were 54 min, 34.8 °C, and 590 mL, respectively.Fig. 3a A

Histopathologic examination of the excised specimen showed the presence of several layers of elastic fibers, but no intimal or medial structures were observed in the saccular pseudoaneurysm. No acute or chronic inflammation was present. Therefore, these findings, clearly revealed a pseudoaneurysm consisting of the adventitia only (Fig. 3b, c).

Several layers of elastic fibers were found (arrow); therefore, a pseudoaneurysm consists of the adventitia only
